title: An Oklahoma football player is turning tackles into a 9/11 tribute
content:
Danny Okoye will spend this fall rooting for an expensive season. Every tackle he records will cost the Oklahoma defensive lineman $100, every sack $200 and every interception $500 — a peculiar accounting system in which the more havoc he creates, the more he’ll owe.

The bill will ultimately be payable to the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, an organization born from the death of Brooklyn, N.Y., firefighter Stephen Siller, who gave his life responding to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center. Twenty-five years later, Okoye — born more than three years after 9/11 — is attaching his junior season to the foundation, which honors Siller’s memory by helping U.S. Armed Forces veterans and first responders secure mortgage-free housing and financial aid.

“You can say that you care about this, care about that, but what are you actually doing to support it?” Okoye, who isn’t receiving any compensation from the foundation, said. “Hopefully, I can put my gifts to use in a way that doesn’t just make my name popular or provide accolades — but actually gives back to something I feel is important.”

Shortly after NIL rules changed in 2021, then-Stanford football player Stuart Head asked Tunnel to Towers about becoming an ambassador. Since then, the foundation has partnered with nearly 30 student-athletes around the nation, but Okoye is the first to link his performance with donations.

“All on him,” said Larry Olson, the organization’s executive vice president of marketing and communications, of Okoye’s idea. “The first time that that ever has happened.”

Service has long occupied a seat at the Okoye family dinner table. His father serves as a chaplain to police and fire stations around Owasso, Okla. One of his paternal uncles is the city’s fire chief; another is a police officer. They often shared stories of wrecks and emergencies, and of pulling strangers from danger.

Last season, after his uncle told Okoye about saving an overdose victim with Narcan, Okoye partnered with a group bringing the medication to college campuses. So when he went searching for his next cause, his family ties made Tunnel to Towers a natural choice.

“This was never … a situation in which he was just looking to align himself with someone that was going to help him in his personal brand,” Olson said.

Though Okoye can’t conjure memories of an event that occurred before he was born, he learned from others about the heroic actions of first responders who rushed to the site of the deadliest terror attack in history — including the 343 members of the New York City Fire Department who died that day.

Okoye, the inquisitive kid who once peppered teachers with questions about the attacks, eventually added history to his studies at Oklahoma.

“The 9/11 event is such an impactful event, but I wasn’t there for it,” he said, “and I’m still seeing the consequences 25 years after.”

This summer, Tunnel to Towers brought a steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center through Oklahoma City as part of a cross-country tour leading up to the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Though Okoye hadn’t partnered with the foundation yet, he squeezed in a visit between football meetings.

Around the beam were stories no history lesson could have taught him. Okoye listened to accounts from survivors, as well as individuals who lost loved ones in the attacks, absorbing so much that the question shifted from what he could learn to what he could teach.

“I started having this new perspective of, ‘Huh, I wonder if other people have the knowledge I have,'” Okoye said. “Maybe I can share a little bit here and there.”

Tunnel to Towers takes its name from the lengths Siller took to reach the World Trade Center site on 9/11. His shift had ended that morning and he had already left the firehouse when he learned that a plane had struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center. He turned around, retrieved his gear from work and drove toward lower Manhattan, but the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel had already been closed to traffic by the time he arrived there. Siller strapped 60 pounds of gear to his back and continued through the tunnel on foot. He reached the World Trade Center and died later that morning when the towers collapsed.

One detail of the firefighter’s story hit Okoye the hardest: Siller had already been off the clock. The consequences of his decision to return, Okoye said, “had me sitting quiet for a little bit.”

“My brother Stephen gave his life running toward danger so that others could live,” Frank Siller, the foundation’s chairman and CEO, said in a statement. “It is people like Danny, who feel that same sense of duty and responsibility, that keep his legacy alive every single day.”

A quarter-century has given new meaning to the “Never Forget” promise woven through Tunnel to Towers’ work. With Sept. 11 slipping further beyond the lived memory of young Americans, Olson said that the foundation’s partnerships with college athletes have become an “ideal way” to reach those born after 2001.

This fall, the Sooners will have a new cheering section some 1,500 miles away in Staten Island, where Olson said Okoye’s fundraiser has created a “scoreboard mentality.”

By season’s end, Okoye hopes the final bill exceeds the havoc he creates on Saturdays. It will measure, in his own small way, what he did with a history he inherited.
